en: The Bodhisattva’s Fivefold Text for Repentance (Translator’s name lost;
now appended to the Liang Dynasty record):
"The Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods, with their five eyes illuminating the world, know all through the three great insights and clearly perceive."
Regarding the characteristics of sin and merit:
we, the disciples [Name] and others, since time immemorial, have failed to encounter virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra) and have committed every kind of transgression.

We have broken the precepts, violating the four grave offenses, the six grave offenses, and the eight grave offenses; we have slandered the Dharma and severed our roots of goodness, fully embodying the nature of an icchantika.

Fortunately, I have encountered the Tathāgatas, the Sūtras and Dharmas, and the assembly of noble sages, who are able to eliminate all transgressions; I, your disciple, prostrate with my head at their feet.
May all clouds of evil be dispelled, and may the unsurpassed wisdom be awakened.
Having finished the repentance, he prostrated with his five limbs touching the ground:

"When the Buddhas of the ten directions first ascended the site of enlightenment, they gazed at the tree and walked in meditation before turning the wheel of Dharma; how lamentable that ignorance and old age and death cause such long-lasting decline!"
I vow to administer the medicine of the Dharma to rescue all from the suffering of illness, and to spread the rain of the Dharma upon withered sentient beings.

Having attained the Way and clearly understood the Buddhas currently present throughout the ten directions, as well as those who have already delivered their有缘 (youyuan—those with whom they share a karmic connection), [the Buddha perceives that] sentient beings are largely indolent; thus, through skillful means, he manifests *nirvāṇa*.
With sincere hearts, we, your disciples, prostrate and entreat the Buddha to remain for a long time.

All the Bodhisattvas, having already resolved upon the supreme aspiration, vow to apply themselves with diligent vigor; in worlds where no Buddha dwells, may they manifest the attainment of Equal and Perfect Enlightenment to universally deliver all sentient beings.
"Compassion and pity are unsurpassed by the Buddha; therefore, I entreat you with a sincere heart.
Having finished his invitation to the Buddha, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and said:

"Throughout successive lifetimes, I have harbored envy and jealousy, as well as pride, anger, and delusion. When I saw others obtain profit, it was as if an arrow pierced my heart; when I heard of others attaining happiness, it was as if a nail were driven into my eyes."
Due to these various karmic obstructions, one falls into the three evil realms and never encounters the Buddhas.

Today, with a single-minded realization, I give rise to a heart of great sympathetic joy toward the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, as well as their assemblies of disciples, whose number is immeasurable.

From the first arising of a single thought until sitting at the site of enlightenment, [the Buddha’s] fourfold great giving, his pure upholding of the prohibitions, his concentration, wisdom, and liberation, and his immeasurable knowledges and insights—all these the disciples followed with complete joy.

The mind of wisdom becomes radiant and clear, and the dark obstructions of ignorance are extinguished; by giving rise to sympathetic joy for a single thought-moment, one's merit fills the ten directions and one’s wisdom becomes equal to that of all Buddhas.
Having finished expressing his sympathetic joy, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground:
"In the cycle of birth and death, from birth until death, and from nobility back to lowliness, I have yet to attain Nirvāṇa."
The Dharma-body is eternally pure, and Prajñā is wondrous liberation; now we shall seek this benefit.
Whatever meritorious deeds there may be, may they all be brought together and dedicated to sentient beings, so that together we may accomplish the Unsurpassed Way.

Vast as space and signless like true wisdom, it extends to the ultimate limits of the Dharma-realm; the vajra-wisdom of emptiness is ever-present, and through the supernormal powers of non-action, there is a response to every invocation.
Having completed the dedication, he prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet and made this great vow with a sincere heart:
"I shall practice the Way according to my vow; may my wisdom-mind be like a fierce wind, and my power of concentration like a diamond."
After this dedication, may every thought-moment transform into compassion; may one abandon thoughts of attachment and joyfully deliver all beings.
When casting off body and life, may the Buddha emit radiance to eliminate all difficulties and obstacles, and may one be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven to behold the Honored One, Maitreya.

Their cultivated marks were fully perfected, and their six sense faculties were universally acute; hearing the Buddha preach the wondrous Dharma, they immediately realized the patience of non-arising and all dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression.

Riding upon the power of great supernatural faculties, they travel throughout the lands of the ten directions, making offerings to all Buddhas with immeasurable and wondrous voices, praising the virtues of the Buddhas.

Within the twenty-five realms of existence, there is no time when he does not manifest his body; like the sun illuminating the world, his radiance brightens the ten directions, serving as a lamp of wisdom in all places of deep darkness.

"Though I attain the Way of the Buddha, turn the wheel of Dharma, and manifest nirvana, as long as sentient beings have not all attained Buddhahood, I shall not abandon the vows of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī.
Having finished making this vow, he purified his mind and paid homage.
The Bodhisattva’s Fivefold Text for Repentance and Confession
